title: Short Stuff: The Mpemba Effect
summary: Short Stuff episode on the Mpemba effect, the counterintuitive observation that hot water can freeze faster than cold water under some conditions. Hosts recount how Erasto Mpemba, a Tanzanian teenager, noticed it while making ice cream in school, how he persuaded visiting British physicist Dennis Osborne to investigate, and how the effect was later named after him. They note earlier mentions by Aristotle, Roger Bacon and Descartes, explain why it seems to violate physical intuition, and discuss the disputed experimental results, the problem of defining "freezing first," an MIT blog post, a 2025 Kyoto measurement standard, and possible applications such as quantum computing cooling and better freezers. A tangent covers a Braves game race against Mister Freeze.
topics: hot water freezes faster than cold water

segments.title: Opening
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the episode on Erasto Mpemba and the Mpemba effect.

segments.title: Opening banter and the effect defined
segments.summary: Brief banter, then the hosts explain the effect: hot liquids can freeze faster than cold ones, and it was noted by Aristotle, Roger Bacon and Descartes before Mpemba.

segments.title: Mpemba's ice cream discovery
segments.summary: As a 13-year-old in Tanzania, Erasto Mpemba noticed hot milk mixtures froze faster in a class ice cream experiment. His teacher dismissed him, and he kept pursuing the idea through school until visiting physicist Dennis Osborne took interest.

segments.title: Osborne collaboration and naming
segments.summary: Osborne invited Mpemba to run experiments, and by 1969 they had written a paper on the phenomenon, which was named after Mpemba.

segments.title: Why the effect seems impossible
segments.summary: The hosts explain that faster-moving molecules would be expected to take longer to cool, so hot water should not reach freezing first. They give an informal example of hot water turning to icy mist in cold weather.
topics: hot water freezes faster than cold water

segments.title: Mister Freeze race analogy
segments.summary: Chuck and Josh use a foot race analogy, and Chuck describes a Braves game where a woman beat a Mister Freeze racer. The tangent ends with talk of Braves games and the team's season.

segments.title: Disputed results
segments.summary: Some experiments have reproduced the effect and others have not. Possible explanations include mineral content, convection currents, and freezer behavior, and some argue it is just an experimental variable.

segments.title: Defining freezing and MIT response
segments.summary: Defining when a liquid counts as frozen is contested. An MIT engineering blog post argued that liquids freeze at the same rate once at freezing temperature, which the hosts say misses the point. A 2025 Kyoto research group created a standard measurement method.

segments.title: Possible unknown forces and applications
segments.summary: Some researchers suggest an unknown physical effect may be involved. Applications discussed include quantum computing qubit cooling, sensors, materials, freezers and refrigerators.

segments.title: Mpemba's later life and sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts note that Erasto Mpemba had a long career as a game warden and died in 2023 at age 73, then close the episode.

segments.summary: Closing lines and the iHeartRadio production credit.
